# Pricing — Charge What It's Worth

**Source:** *$100M Offers*, "Pricing: Charge What It's Worth" + "Value-Driven vs. Price-Driven"
money-math (lines ~569–657, ~847–1075). `hormozi-offer-pricing` uses this to set a premium price
*after* value is built. The governing quote:

> "Charge as high a price as you can say out loud without cracking a smile." — Dan Kennedy (l.849)

**Core stance:** the objective is **not** to get the most customers — it's to make the most money
(l.965). "99% of businesses need to raise their prices to grow, not lower them. **Profit is oxygen**"
(l.1073). Raise price only **after** value is high enough that the buyer still gets a steal.

---

## Value-driven vs. price-driven purchases (why differentiation lets you charge more)

- **Commoditized → price-driven purchase → race to the bottom.** "A commodity is a product available
  from many places," so if products look "equal," the cheapest wins by default; the market drives price
  to the point of efficiency where margins are "just enough to keep the lights on" (l.577–583).
- **Differentiated → value-driven purchase → a category of one.** A Grand Slam Offer "cannot be compared
  to any other product or service," so the decision is between your offer **and nothing** — "you can
  sell at whatever price you get the prospect to perceive, not in comparison to anything else" (l.591–593).

A Grand Slam Offer lifts all three growth levers — **(1) increased response rates (clicks), (2)
increased conversion (sales), (3) premium prices** (l.595–599) — while "the fulfillment is the same" in
both cases (l.607). The offer, not the product, changes the buyer's value-meter.

### The before/after money math (l.611–657)
Real lead-gen-agency numbers, rounded for illustration:
- **Old commoditized way:** $1,000 down + $1,000/mo retainer. At 0.5–1× return on ad spend you *lose*
  money acquiring customers; you break even only when the 5 customers pay again in 30 days ($10,000
  total), and the *next* month's $5,000 is your first profit (l.619–621).
- **New Grand Slam Offer way:** pay once, no retainer, just cover ad spend; performance-based; a
  guarantee ("20 people your first month or your next month free") + the full industry playbook free
  (l.639–647).
- **Multiplier:** same spend/eyeballs → **2.5× more respond × 2.5× more convert × 4× higher price up
  front = 22.4× more cash collected up front** — "you spent $10,000 to make $112,000. You just *made
  money* getting new customers" (l.653). *(Context: first 18 months $500k/yr → $28M/yr on <$1M ad spend;
  20:1–100:1 returns, l.657.)*

**Pricing takeaway:** the 4× price is only *collectable* because response × conversion were lifted by
differentiation — premium price rides on a differentiated, incomparable offer, not on a bare number.

---

## Price-to-value discrepancy (the thing to protect)

People buy to get a **deal**: they believe VALUE received > PRICE paid. "The moment the value dips below
what they're paying, they stop buying" — avoid that discrepancy at all costs (l.929).

> "Price is what you pay. Value is what you get." — Warren Buffett (l.931)

The simplest way to widen the value–price gap is to **lower price** — and it's "most of the time the
wrong decision" (l.933). Lowering price is a one-way road: "you can only go down to $0, but you can go
infinitely high in the other direction" (l.935).

> "There is no strategic benefit to being the second cheapest in the marketplace, but there is for being
> the most expensive." — Dan Kennedy (l.937)

**The rule:** widen the gap by **raising value first, then raising price** — so the buyer still gets
"$100,000 of value for $10,000," i.e., **"money at a discount"** (l.939). Don't compete on price unless
you have a genuine way to cut your costs to ~1/10 of competitors' (l.935).

### Why "charge so much it hurts" — the typical pricing trap
Most owners don't compete on value **or** price — they: (1) look at the market, (2) copy competitors,
(3) take the average, (4) go slightly below to seem "competitive," (5) add "a little more," landing at
"more for less" (l.947–959). "The big secret: those competitors they're copying are **dead broke** — so
why copy them?" (l.961). Market efficiency then grinds everyone to "just above what it costs to stay
above water," washing out the bottom 10–20% (l.963). Premium pricing is the escape — Hormozi frames it
as not just smart but **moral**, because only healthy margin lets you actually deliver.

---

## The Virtuous Cycle of Price (the central pricing framework)

Price is not just capture — it changes the *outcome the client gets.*

**Vicious cycle — when you DECREASE price (l.973–991):**
- ↓ client's **emotional investment** (it didn't cost them much)
- ↓ client's **perceived value** (can't be good if it's cheap / priced like everyone)
- ↓ client's **results** (they don't value it and aren't invested)
- attracts the **worst clients** — never satisfied until it's free
- **destroys margin** → can't fund an exceptional experience, best people, scale → your world and your
  service both "suck"; you join the army racing to the bottom.

**Virtuous cycle — when you RAISE price (l.995–1007):**
- ↑ client's **emotional investment**
- ↑ client's **perceived value**
- ↑ client's **results** (they value it and are invested)
- attracts the **best clients** — easiest to satisfy, cost *less* to fulfill, perceive the most value
- **multiplies margin** → invest in systems, talent, experience, scale → bank balance climbs even while
  reinvesting → you help more people for the long haul.

**Investment → adherence → results (the moral core, l.1021):** if the client must *do* something to get
the result, they must be **invested**. Price it so it **stings** a little — "Those who pay the most, pay
the most attention." More adherent clients get better results, so a premium price literally makes you
deliver *more* value than a cheaper competitor. **Caveat:** this only holds if "your product must
*deliver*" — premium price demands conviction earned by having done it many times ("outwork your
self-doubt," l.1023).

---

## Higher Price Means Higher Value (literally)

Raising price can **increase the value the consumer receives without changing the product** (l.1009).
*Wine study pattern:* tasters rated three "different" wines by price — most expensive = "best," cheapest
= "cheap wine" — but researchers poured the **same wine** all three times; price alone moved perceived
quality (l.1013–1015). Implications:
- Higher price adds **allure** — "People *want* to buy expensive things. They just need a reason"
  (l.1017).
- Don't aim slightly above market — aim **so far above** that the prospect thinks *"this is so much more
  expensive, there must be something entirely different going on here."* That perception **creates the
  category of one** → a perceived monopoly → **monopoly profits** (l.1017–1019).

---

## Premium-price worked pattern (Gym Launch)

Setting the anchor high (l.1037–1043): market had low-price competitors at **$500/mo** and one
high-price player at **$5,000**. Hormozi deliberately became the premium leader — **$16,000 for a
16-week done-with-you intensive** (~3× the highest player, ~32× the low players) — then upsold **35%**
into a **3-year, $42,000/year** agreement. Context: the average gym owner takes home **$35,280/year**,
so many were committing **half their annual pay or more** — sold on **conviction over their skepticism**.

The conviction was earned by results (158-gym survey, ~11 months in program, l.1045–1059):
- Top-line revenue **+$19,932/mo (+$239,000/yr)**
- Recurring revenue **+$13,339/mo (+$160,068/yr)**
- Bottom-line profit **$2,943/mo → $8,940/mo (3.1×)**
- Clients **+67**; churn **10.7% → 6.8%**; retail **+$4,400/mo**; member price **$129 → $167/mo**

**Pattern to reuse:** price at a large multiple of the *highest* incumbent (not a hair above the
average), justify it by charging a **fraction of what the client will make** (they still get a deal),
and back it with proof + guarantee so conviction outweighs skepticism.

---

## Pricing decision rules (summary)

1. **Build value first; raise price second** — never lead with price to widen the gap.
2. **Never be the 2nd-cheapest** — either be a genuine cost-leader (~1/10 cost) or be the premium leader.
3. **Anchor off the highest incumbent, by a multiple** — high enough to trigger the "something entirely
   different" perception (category of one).
4. **Price so it stings** — enough to force investment/attention (drives client results), while the
   value delivered still makes it a steal ("money at a discount").
5. **Protect the value–price discrepancy** — if you ever must move price, move *value* first.
6. **Conviction gate** — only charge premium if the product genuinely delivers; proof + guarantee carry
   the price.

---

## Output contract (for `hormozi-offer-pricing`)

Given the built offer + market, produce:
1. A recommended **premium price** (and any upsell/continuity tier), anchored as a **multiple of the
   highest incumbent** with the anchor named — figures derived from the product's real economics or
   marked `<placeholder>`; **no fabricated numbers**.
2. The **value-to-price gap** stated so the buyer still gets a steal ("$X value for $Y price").
3. A **Virtuous-Cycle rationale** (why this price improves client results, not just revenue) and the
   **conviction/proof** required to hold it.
4. An explicit **anti-discount warning** if the user is tempted to compete on price, with the
   race-to-the-bottom consequence spelled out.
5. Flag every price/number as product-derived vs. assumption; mark placeholders to fill.

Dan Kennedy "cracking a smile" (l.849); Price-to-Value Discrepancy + Buffett + "no benefit to 2nd
